Name: microbial_mediation_antagonistic_pleiotropy
Title: Transient Soil Microbiota as Mediators of Antagonistic Pleiotropy in Plant Local Adaptation
Experiment: We will build a gnotobiotic experimental system using Brassica rapa. First, we will create two defined soil microbial communities extracted from limestone and tuff field sites, each subjected to whole‑community metagenomic sequencing and selective sterilization to generate ‘home’ and ‘away’ inocula. Second, we will run a 10‑generation experimental evolution in a factorial design: Soil type (limestone/tuff) × microbial treatment (sterile, native microbiota, cross‑inoculated microbiota, and ‘pulsed’ microbiota where communities are removed via mild heat/antibiotic treatment after generation 5) × herbivory (aphids present/absent) × pollination (bumblebee/hand). At generation 10, a full reciprocal transplant experiment will measure lifetime fitness (seed set) across all previous environments. We will perform whole‑genome sequencing of each population to detect allele frequency shifts and identify SNPs exhibiting environment‑dependent pleiotropy. For candidate loci, we will use CRISPR‑Cas9 knockout lines to test fitness effects in microcosms with and without microbial partners. Metrics: relative fitness, selection coefficients, allele frequency change, and gene expression of defense‑ and growth‑related genes. Baselines: original 8‑generation experiment without microbial manipulation. Expected outcomes: (1) The presence of co‑adapted soil microbiota is required for antagonistic pleiotropy to manifest; removal after 5 generations shifts loci towards conditional neutrality. (2) Cross‑inoculation reduces local adaptation and erodes trade‑offs. Ablation studies: vary the timing of microbial removal (generations 3, 5, 7), the complexity of inocula (whole community vs. synthetic consortia of key taxa), and measure microbial recolonization dynamics.
Abstract: The mechanisms driving local adaptation in plants are often framed as a dichotomy between antagonistic pleiotropy and conditional neutrality, yet the role of the soil microbiome in shaping these genetic architectures remains untested. Here we integrate gnotobiotic soil systems with multi‑generation experimental evolution in Brassica rapa to dissect whether soil microbiota act as transient intermediaries that sustain pleiotropic trade-offs. We evolved replicate lines on limestone and tuff soils in the presence or absence of native microbial communities and under factorial herbivory and pollination treatments, with pulsed removal of microbiota at mid‑experiment. After ten generations, reciprocal transplants revealed that local adaptation and the signature of antagonistic pleiotropy at previously identified loci depend on the continuous presence of co‑adapted microbiota; once removed, those alleles became conditionally neutral. CRISPR‑validated lines showed that the fitness costs of pleiotropic alleles are mediated by microbial induction of root defense pathways, linking growth‑defense trade‑offs to the rhizosphere. Our findings reveal that soil microbes function as keystone mediators of eco‑evolutionary feedbacks, challenging the view that local adaptation is solely dictated by abiotic and macro‑biotic interactions.
Method:
1. Gnotobiotic Microbiome Construction and Management: Collect soil from limestone and tuff field sites, extract total microbiota, and sequence metagenomes to define ‘home’ communities. Sterilize seeds and soil matrices by gamma irradiation. Re‑inoculate sterile soils with either the total native community, a cross‑inoculation from the opposite soil, or a sterile control. For ‘pulsed’ treatments, apply mild heat (40°C) and selective antibiotics after generation 5 to collapse the microbial community, followed by re‑sterilization; resilience is monitored via qPCR and 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing.
2. Multi‑Generation Experimental Evolution: Using the full factorial design (2 soil types × 4 microbial treatments × 2 herbivory levels × 2 pollination modes), maintain 5 replicate populations per combination (160 populations) for 10 generations under controlled growth chambers. At each generation, record phenology and fitness components (seed set). Preserve leaf and root tissue for RNA‑seq and DNA extraction.
3. Reciprocal Transplant and Genome Analysis: After 10 generations, perform a common‑garden transplant of all populations into all four microbial × soil environments. Measure lifetime fitness (germination to seed production) and calculate local adaptation indices. Conduct pooled whole‑genome sequencing of each population at generation 0 and 10 to identify SNPs with significant allele frequency changes. Classify SNPs as antagonistically pleiotropic if the allele has opposite fitness effects across soil types only in the presence of native microbiota.
4. Functional Validation: Select top antagonistic candidate SNPs in defense‑ and nutrient‑related genes. Generate isogenic knockout and overexpression lines via CRISPR‑Cas9. Test these lines in microcosms with manipulated microbial presence, measuring gene expression via RNA‑seq and growth‑defense trade‑offs via glucosinolate content and biomass. Confirm that microbial cues directly regulate the expression of the pleiotropic loci.
